---
title: "Case Study: Cursor's Continual Training Loop"
---

## The Question

Cursor frequently updates Tab and Composer from production interaction data.
This makes them useful case studies for three questions:

1. How can a deployed model generate its next round of training data?
2. Why use reinforcement learning instead of only next-token prediction?
3. Does changing the objective to RL solve catastrophic forgetting?

The short answer to the third question is **no**. RL improves alignment between
training signal and product utility. Retention still depends on the task
mixture, replay or anchoring distribution, regularization, and regression
evaluation.

This note reconstructs only what Cursor has publicly disclosed. Details such as
the complete data mixture, reward weights, replay policy, and all
anti-forgetting mechanisms remain private.

## Two Meanings of Continual Learning

Cursor's public loops implement **population-level online model improvement**:

$$
\text{deploy checkpoint}
\rightarrow
\text{collect population feedback}
\rightarrow
\text{train next checkpoint}
\rightarrow
\text{evaluate and redeploy}.
$$

This differs from a model updating private weights during one user's lifetime:

| Form | Persistent state | Timescale |
|---|---|---|
| Cursor's real-time training | shared model checkpoint | hours to model releases |
| within-session adaptation | context, cache, files, or memory | seconds to hours |
| lifelong personalized learning | user-specific persistent memory or weights | months to years |

The distinction matters when connecting this case to
[continual intelligence](../advanced/continual_intelligence_ttt.qmd). Cursor is
closing the outer product-training loop, not claiming to solve every layer of
lifelong memory.

## Cursor Tab: Learn Whether an Action Is Worth Showing

Tab observes a state $s$ containing the codebase, cursor location, and recent
interaction. Its action is not merely a token continuation. It can:

- propose an edit
- propose a cursor jump or subsequent edit
- abstain and show nothing

User acceptance or rejection supplies a reward. Cursor repeatedly deploys a
checkpoint, collects fresh actions and outcomes, applies a policy-gradient
update, and deploys the next checkpoint:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    P[Current Tab policy] --> D[Deploy]
    D --> I[User interactions]
    I --> R[Accept / reject / abstain rewards]
    R --> U[Policy-gradient update]
    U --> E[Regression and product evaluation]
    E --> P2[Next policy]
```

### Why abstention makes this a decision problem

Suppose the illustrative rewards are

$$
R(\text{accept})=0.75,
\qquad
R(\text{reject})=-0.25,
\qquad
R(\text{abstain})=0.
$$

If a suggestion has acceptance probability $p$, showing it has expected reward

$$
0.75p-0.25(1-p)=p-0.25.
$$

The optimal policy therefore shows the suggestion only when $p>0.25$. Changing
the reward changes the implicit threshold. The model learns generation and
filtering as one policy rather than relying only on a separately trained
acceptance classifier.

Cursor reports collecting a new checkpoint's on-policy data in roughly
1.5--2 hours. Its disclosed result made fewer suggestions while increasing the
acceptance rate. See
[Improving Cursor Tab with online RL](https://cursor.com/blog/tab-rl).

### Why not train only on the user's next edit?

NTP or behavior cloning would answer:

> Given this context, what action did the user take?

Tab's product objective is closer to:

> Given the action this policy would propose, was showing it useful enough to
> interrupt the user?

One logged user edit is not the only acceptable continuation. It also does not
directly label the counterfactual value of showing a particular model-generated
suggestion. Acceptance, rejection, suggestion length, jumps, and abstention are
more naturally expressed as action-dependent utility.

## Composer: Knowledge First, Agent Policy Second

Composer does not replace language-model training with RL. Composer 2 uses a
staged pipeline:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    B[Kimi K2.5 base] --> C[Code-heavy continued pretraining]
    C --> L[Long-context extension]
    L --> S[Targeted SFT]
    S --> R[Asynchronous agentic RL]
    R --> O[Real-time production RL]
```

The stages solve different problems:

| Stage | Primary role |
|---|---|
| continued pretraining | acquire code knowledge and lower code perplexity |
| long-context training | operate on larger codebases and histories |
| targeted SFT | initialize useful instruction and tool behavior |
| simulated agent RL | optimize multi-step problem solving in a controlled harness |
| production RL | reduce simulator–user mismatch using real outcomes |

Cursor reports that lower continued-pretraining cross-entropy predicts better
downstream RL performance. This is evidence against the idea that agentic RL
makes NTP obsolete. A knowledgeable base makes a better policy learner. See the
[Composer 2 technical report](https://cursor.com/resources/Composer2.pdf).

### Simulated agentic RL

Composer receives realistic coding tasks and the same classes of tools used in
the deployed [agent harness](harness.qmd): file reading and editing, terminal
commands, grep, semantic search, and web search. Multiple trajectories are
sampled, executed in sandboxed environments, and updated according to solution
quality.

The disclosed task distribution includes new features, debugging, refactoring,
codebase understanding, documentation, testing, review, optimization, DevOps,
migration, and deletion. Task breadth is important: a narrow stream of one task
type would make specialization and forgetting much harder to distinguish.

Composer 2 updates the full parameter set, operates in a single-epoch regime,
uses KL regularization, and tries to keep asynchronous rollouts close to the
current policy through frequent weight synchronization and MoE-routing replay.

### Real-time RL

Cursor later closes the loop with production use:

$$
\text{billions of interaction tokens}
\rightarrow
\text{derived reward signals}
\rightarrow
\text{full-weight update}
\rightarrow
\text{regression suites}
\rightarrow
\text{deployment}.
$$

Cursor reports that this cycle can produce a candidate checkpoint in about five
hours. Before deployment, the model is checked against CursorBench and other
evaluation suites. Production monitoring revealed reward hacks such as
intentionally invalid tool calls and excessive clarification instead of editing;
the reward and data pipeline then had to be corrected. See
[Improving Composer through real-time RL](https://cursor.com/blog/real-time-rl-for-composer).

This is best understood as a **closed-loop product optimizer**. The reward is
not a fact about the world; it is an evolving measurement system built from user
behavior, environment outcomes, latency, persistence of edits, and product
judgment.

## Composer 2.5: RL and Distillation Are Composed {#sec-composer-distillation}

Long trajectories make credit assignment difficult: a final reward may reveal
that the rollout was poor without identifying the bad turn. Composer 2.5 adds
targeted textual feedback:

1. locate a problematic message or tool decision
2. insert a short corrective hint into that local context
3. treat the hint-conditioned model distribution as a teacher
4. apply an on-policy KL loss from the original-context student toward that
   teacher
5. retain the broader trajectory-level RL objective

This combines sparse outcome optimization with dense local supervision:

$$
\mathcal L
=
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{RL}}
+
\lambda
\operatorname{KL}
\left(
\pi_{\text{teacher with hint}}
\middle\|
\pi_{\theta,\text{original context}}
\right).
$$

It is a concrete instance of the distinction in
[Distillation: Learning from a Teacher](../foundations/distillation.qmd): the
state distribution, teacher construction, KL direction, and trajectory reward
are separate design choices. See
[Introducing Composer 2.5](https://cursor.com/blog/composer-2-5).

## RL and NTP Differ in Credit, Not Memory Safety

For a demonstrated action $a^*$, NTP/SFT applies

$$
\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_{\mathrm{NTP}}
=
-\mathbb E
\left[
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a^*\mid s)
\right].
$$

A policy gradient applies

$$
\nabla_\theta J
=
\mathbb E_{s,a\sim\pi_\theta}
\left[
A(s,a)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)
\right].
$$

Both change log probabilities in the same shared parameters. RL changes which
actions receive positive or negative weight and permits sequence-level,
action-dependent credit. Nothing in this equation automatically protects an
old capability whose states are absent from the new training distribution.

This illustrates the four-axis framework in
[Losses from First Principles](../foundations/losses.qmd):

| Axis | NTP/SFT | Online RL |
|---|---|---|
| learned object | conditional next-action distribution | utility-maximizing policy |
| supervision | observed target action | environment or user reward |
| discrepancy | log loss | advantage-weighted log probability |
| state distribution | usually logged/static contexts | current policy's encountered states |

## Why RL Does Not Solve Catastrophic Forgetting

Catastrophic forgetting occurs when updates that improve the current training
distribution damage behavior required on earlier or absent distributions. Both
NTP and RL can cause it:

$$
\nabla L_{\text{new}}^T\nabla L_{\text{old}}<0
$$

indicates local gradient interference. RL can make the problem worse when its
reward is narrow, noisy, or exploitable: policy entropy can collapse, a single
tool strategy can dominate, or measurable behavior can displace unmeasured
skills.

A KL penalty can limit behavioral drift:

$$
\max_\theta
\mathbb E_{\tau\sim\pi_\theta}[R(\tau)]
-
\beta
\mathbb E_{s\sim\mu}
\operatorname{KL}
\left(
\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s)
\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid s)
\right).
$$

But this protects behavior only on anchor states $s\sim\mu$. If an old skill is
missing from $\mu$, the KL term does not directly test it. KL is a trust region,
not a complete memory system.

## What Actually Provides Retention?

Cursor has not disclosed or claimed a complete solution to catastrophic
forgetting. The public recipe exposes several practical defenses:

| Mechanism | What it protects | What it cannot guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| broad task distribution | coverage across common coding workflows | unrelated or rare skills |
| KL to a reference policy | local behavioral stability on anchor states | retention off the anchor distribution |
| small, frequent on-policy cycles | lower policy lag and easier diagnosis | absence of long-run feedback loops |
| single-epoch RL prompts | less memorization of individual tasks | no interference across tasks |
| regression and held-out evaluations | measured capabilities before deployment | unmeasured capabilities |
| reward monitoring and A/B tests | production regressions and reward hacks | delayed or weakly observed harms |

A more general continual-learning system may additionally need:

- replay mixing historical, general, and current data
- teacher-logit distillation on a stable anchor suite
- adapters or separated plastic/stable parameters
- explicit gradient-conflict management
- checkpoint rollback and population-level canaries
- a policy for deciding which episodes deserve weight consolidation

The exact replay and retention mixture used internally by Cursor is not public,
so it should not be inferred from the existence of online RL.

## The First-Principles Interpretation

Cursor's main innovation is not “RL remembers better.” It is a tight match among
four components:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    P[Production state distribution]
    A[Current policy actions]
    F[Real user and environment feedback]
    G[Frequent guarded updates]
    P --> A --> F --> G --> P
```

The loop reduces three mismatches:

1. **state mismatch:** train on states the deployed policy actually encounters
2. **action mismatch:** evaluate the model's own suggestions and trajectories
3. **objective mismatch:** optimize acceptance and task outcome rather than only
   imitation likelihood

It simultaneously creates three risks:

1. **feedback loops:** the policy changes the data it later observes
2. **reward hacking:** measured proxies become optimization targets
3. **forgetting:** current high-volume behaviors can dominate older or rarer
   capabilities

Thus continual product learning requires a second, slower loop that audits the
fast learning loop. This is where harness observability, regression suites,
reward design, replay, and rollback become part of the learning algorithm.

## Interview Questions

- Why is Tab's abstention decision difficult to express as ordinary NTP?
- Derive the acceptance threshold implied by positive, negative, and abstention
  rewards.
- Why must Tab refresh its data after updating the policy?
- Separate Composer's continued pretraining, SFT, simulated RL, and real-time RL
  objectives.
- Why does lower code perplexity still help downstream agentic RL?
- Why does RL not inherently prevent catastrophic forgetting?
- What does a KL penalty preserve, and how does its state distribution limit the
  guarantee?
- How does Composer 2.5 combine trajectory reward with localized on-policy
  distillation?
- Which regression suite would detect a policy becoming better at editing but
  worse at explanation, planning, or abstention?
- Is Cursor's loop lifelong learning, online learning, or continual product
  optimization? State the timescale and persistent state in your answer.
